r.정치 구도: Kazakhstan is a presidential system with power heavily concentrated in the president. One leader ran the country for nearly 30 years after independence in 1991 and kept much of his influence for a while after stepping down in 2019. In January 2022, protests against a fuel price hike spread nationwide, more than 200 people were killed, and troops from a Russia-led security bloc were brought in. Afterward, the former leader's camp was pushed aside, and the constitution was amended to limit the president to a single seven-year term. A new constitution approved by referendum in March 2026 abolished the Senate, created a single-chamber parliament called the Kurultai and restored the post of vice president. The government calls these reforms, but opposition parties and the media remain tightly constrained.

t.why: The world's largest landlocked country shares a border of more than 7,000 km with Russia and also borders China. It mines about 40% of the world's uranium, making it the top producer and important to countries expanding nuclear power. It has giant oil fields such as Tengiz and Kashagan, but most of its crude exports run through a pipeline to a Russian Black Sea port, a route that has faced attacks and disruptions since the war in Ukraine. That is why it is building up the Middle Corridor across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey. Although it belongs to the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union and Collective Security Treaty Organization, it has not endorsed the invasion of Ukraine and has said it will respect Western sanctions. China first announced its Belt and Road Initiative in the Kazakh capital in 2013, a sign of the country's role as the key land bridge between China and Europe.
t.rel: It shares one of the longest borders in the world with Russia. A member of Russia-led economic and security blocs, it pursues 'multi-vector' diplomacy, widening ties with China and the West as well.
t.korea: The two countries established diplomatic relations in 1992. A Koryo-saram community took root in Kazakhstan after the Soviet Union forcibly deported ethnic Koreans from the Russian Far East to Central Asia in 1937, and more than 100,000 still live there. In 2021 the remains of independence fighter General Hong Beom-do, who had been buried there, were brought back to South Korea. More than 700 Korean companies operate in Kazakhstan, and a 2024 critical-minerals supply chain partnership committed the two sides to jointly explore for lithium and other minerals. In September 2026 they upgraded ties to a 'future-oriented comprehensive strategic partnership' and agreed to expand crude oil imports and nuclear cooperation. At the same time, Kazakhstan was added as a sending country under South Korea's Employment Permit System, opening a path for its workers.
t.know: Kazakhstan's Baikonur Cosmodrome, where Gagarin launched into space in 1961, is still leased by Russia.
etext: The giant Tengiz, Kashagan and Karachaganak fields are developed with American and European oil companies. Uranium is extracted by pumping solution underground to dissolve the ore, which keeps costs low, and state-owned Kazatomprom is the world's largest producer.

Its minerals range from copper, zinc, iron ore and chromium to rare earths. South Korea, Europe and the United States, all looking for critical minerals outside China, have been signing cooperation deals one after another.
Companies such as Kaspi have bundled payments, shopping and loans into a single app that many people use every day. The government has also moved many public services online.
The economy swings with oil prices, and export routes through Russia carry political risk. Many large companies are in the hands of the state or a few families, and critics say competition is weak.
